title: get
description: One command for the terminal's common reflexes: what you hand `get` decides what it does — a directory gets listed, a file gets displayed, a word gets grepped, a loose query over a folder becomes a filename search with an fzf pick, `+` watches a file live, `@` opens the editor, and `-` forces a plain stdout view. The `get` function also owns the cd flow, so cd+ls is one step.

content.heading: get - fast cd+ls workflow for folders, with file viewing and search
content: `get` is a traversal-first helper for the terminal: most invocations are a single `get` away from where you are, and the `-` back-navigation keeps a history of the directories you've been in. The purpose of `get` is to make the cd+ls workflow fast for folders — and it additionally provides support for viewing files in bat, cat, and vim, and supports reading links/PATH items.

`get` is implemented as a bash function (for cd support), backed by `got` — the POSIX-sh script holding all the logic (listing, cat/bat display, grep, filename search + fzf picking, `$PATH` resolution).

`@<name>` is interactive-first: it opens the file in `$EDITOR`, resolving `$PATH` commands and symlinks to the real file; when the session is not a tty (stdin or stdout is piped, as in `cat "$(get @x)"`), it prints the canonical resolved path instead. `+<name>` is the watcher: it execs into `blitch view` — the inotify-based, colour-coded live pager — and `got` is gone; no polling happens in `got` at all. Without blitch on PATH — or when the target is a folder, or extra arguments are present — it degrades to exactly the editor action. `-<name>` forces a plain stdout view of that one argument, wherever it appears (before `--`), winning over the editor, the watch, and the query split.

content.heading: Usage
content: get                              ls -al the current directory
get +<name> [more...]            watch <name> live via blitch view (the colour-coded inotify pager); without blitch — or for a folder or extra args — degrade to the editor action
get @<name> [more...]            open <name> in $EDITOR; if not a local file, resolve it on $PATH and follow symlinks to the real file; non-interactive callers get the resolved path(s) printed
get @                            ls the current directory, then find extra names beneath it
get -<name> [more...]            force a plain stdout view of each -prefixed argument (any position before "--"; wins over +, @, grep)
got <dir> [names...]             ls the dir, then find each name beneath it
got <file...>                    cat/bat the files
got <queries...> <file|dir>      grep each query (with file+line numbers); for a folder, find matching filenames and fzf-pick one
got <queries...> -- <file|dir>…  same, with an explicit queries/targets split
got -n <queries...> <dir>        filename search + fzf pick
get -                            cd to the previous directory first
get <dir> [names...]             cd into <dir>, then behave like `got .`

content.heading: Split rule
content: Without `--`: an argument that exists as a file/dir is a target, everything else is a query. If there are no queries at all, targets are displayed; if there are queries, targets are searched.

content.heading: Implementation
content: `get` is implemented as a bash function (for cd support), backed by `got` — the POSIX-sh script holding all the logic (listing, cat/bat display, grep, filename search + fzf picking, `$PATH` resolution, the `+`/`-`/`@` prefixes).

Watching owns no polling in `got`: `+<name>` execs into `blitch view` — a live pager whose inotify watcher observes the file's parent directory filtered by basename, so editor-style atomic saves (temp file + rename over the original) cannot kill the watch, with a 40 ms trailing-edge debounce coalescing one save's event burst into a single redraw. Without blitch on PATH — or for folder targets and extra arguments — the watch degrades to the editor action.

content.heading: Why two names
content: `got` is a POSIX-sh script, `get` is a thin bash/zsh function wrapping it — a subprocess can't `cd` for you, so the function owns the cd-then-list flow while `got` holds all the viewing/searching logic. The `@<name>` opener degrades gracefully: interactive, it opens `$EDITOR`; piped (scripts, agents, `cat "$(get @x)"`), it prints the canonical resolved path instead — and bare `get -` still cds to the previous directory before anything else runs.

content.heading: Requirements
content: blitch — the inotify-based colour-coded live pager behind `+` watching; without it the watch degrades to the editor action. bat — richer file display; without it, plain cat is used. fzf — the pick UI for folder filename search; without it the search still prints matches.

content.heading: Install
content: make install          # ~/.local prefix — distributes files only, never edits rc files

The shell extension is wired by sourcing the deployed hook ONCE from your rc file (add the line yourself; dots machines wire it via ~/.shellx.rc): [ -f "$HOME/.local/share/got/hook.sh" ] && . "$HOME/.local/share/got/hook.sh"

An existing hook.sh is preserved on install (theirs wins); make install FORCE=1 clobbers it with the shipped default (the upgrade path). The repo's hook.sh is a gitignored path, force-add tracked and skip-worktree'd, so per-machine content and local tweaks stay out of git status. Knobs: PREFIX=..., DESTDIR=... (staging), SKIP_RC=1 (skip the wiring report), RC_FILES="..." (wiring-report scope). make uninstall removes the owned files — the rc line goes inert automatically; make uninstall-rc strips LEGACY marker blocks from old installs; make check smoke-tests the tree.
